title: A cross-sectional look at teacher reactions, worries, and professional development needs related to generative AI in an urban school district
extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers in a large urban school district reacted to generative AI, especially chatbot tools such as ChatGPT, shortly after their widespread emergence. The study asks what factors shape teacher willingness to allow student use of generative AI for different academic tasks, what concerns and benefits teachers associate with AI for themselves versus students, and what professional development needs teachers identify. The motivation is to understand early teacher perceptions and implementation barriers in a context where schools are rapidly forming policies but empirical evidence remains limited.

The authors used a district-wide survey embedded in the annual employee survey for certificated educators. Responses from 1,454 teachers were analyzed using a mixed-methods design that combined logistic regression on closed-ended items with thematic coding of open-ended responses. Teachers reported whether they had used chatbots recently, whether they allowed student use for specific tasks, and what concerns, benefits, and training needs they had. The sample came from one large West Coast urban district serving elementary, middle, and high school levels.

Findings show that willingness to allow generative AI decreased as grade level increased: high school teachers were generally more restrictive than elementary teachers, and more experienced teachers were also more likely to disallow use. Teachers were especially concerned about overreliance, plagiarism, and misinformation, with these concerns differing between teacher use and student use. Teachers also saw different benefits for themselves and students, and reported grade-specific professional development needs: elementary and middle school teachers wanted foundational AI literacy, while high school teachers emphasized how to manage student use and detect AI-generated work. Overall, the paper concludes that teachers are cautious about generative AI, and that policy and professional development should be tailored by grade level and instructional context.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI chatbot technology used for text generation, concept explanation, and related academic assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Surveyed K-12 teachers’ reactions, concerns, benefits, and professional development needs related to generative AI chatbots in schools, with examples explicitly including ChatGPT as an instance of the category.

findings.finding_summary: In a cross-sectional survey of 1,454 teachers in a large urban district, teachers were less willing to allow generative AI use as grade level increased. The probability of allowing AI chatbot use decreased from elementary to middle/high school across idea generation, paper editing, full-paper writing, concept explanation, and code generation, with the largest disallowance for editing/completing a paper.
findings.measure: Teacher allowability/policy toward student use of AI chatbots for five academic tasks
findings.effect_size: dy/dx ranging from -0.117 to -0.150 for grade level; elementary more-experienced teacher dy/dx = -0.489, -0.502, -0.587 for idea generation, editing, and full-paper writing
findings.confidence_interval: grade-level models: [0.025, 0.975] ranges reported in tables; e.g. -0.126 to -0.116, -0.125 to -0.108, -0.138 to -0.132, -0.133 to -0.117, -0.156 to -0.144; exact CIs vary by outcome
findings.sample_size: n=1,454; outcome-specific N ranges from 24 to 254 depending on task/model

findings.finding_summary: Teachers’ qualitative concerns emphasized overreliance, misinformation, and plagiarism/misuse. Overreliance was the most frequently named concern for both teachers and students, and teachers especially associated student AI use with plagiarism/misuse and overreliance.
findings.measure: Open-ended concern coding from teacher survey responses
findings.sample_size: n=668 for teachers’ concerns; n=669 for students’ concerns

findings.finding_summary: Teachers saw different benefits for teachers versus students. For teachers, commonly cited benefits included preparing lesson plans/materials (21.41%) and increased efficiency (13.62%); for students, the most common benefit was information retrieval/searching (20.33%).
findings.measure: Open-ended benefit coding from teacher survey responses
findings.sample_size: n=626 for teachers’ benefits; n=630 for students’ benefits

findings.finding_summary: Professional development needs varied significantly by grade level but not by subject or experience. Teachers most often wanted guidance on appropriately using AI for pedagogical purposes, while high school teachers especially wanted help with instructing/managing student AI use and detecting AI-generated work.
findings.measure: Open-ended professional development needs and chi-square comparisons across grade levels/subjects/experience
findings.sample_size: n=1,454 overall; qualitative need proportions reported for grade-level subsamples

quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional mixed-methods survey study with descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and logistic regression, but no experimental or longitudinal design. Evidence is useful for documenting teacher perceptions and concerns, yet it cannot establish causal effects of generative AI use.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports substantial attitudinal differences and clear concerns, but not effect sizes for learning outcomes or direct harm from the tool itself. Findings indicate important adoption barriers and cautionary perceptions rather than demonstrated positive or negative achievement impact.
